title: Inference reading routine + annotated takeaways
content:
Purpose and how I use this doc:
- Quick personal ritual to digest 1–3 inference papers / posts per week and capture runnable ideas.
- Keep a prioritized micro-experiments list that I can hand off to interns or run quickly on a single A100.
- Capture heuristics that might feed Redwood Optimize recommendations.

Reading cadence this sprint:
- Focus themes: KV cache eviction strategies, quantization-stability failure modes, cheap latency-aware batching.
- 4 deep reads this week (papers + 2 blogs). Annotated below with my raw takeaways.

1) "Sparse eviction for long-context caching" (paper, arXiv) — notes
- What they did: lightweight scoring for cache entries using recency + token-level importance (attention-weight proxy). Evict low-score spans rather than LRU at token granularity.
- Key result: ~15–25% fewer clarification prompts on long-dialog benchmarks at same mem budget; throughput unchanged.
- My reaction: promising for chat workloads where topical spans have different salience. LRU is too crude when context contains many low-value tokens (boilerplate).
- Questions / caveats:
  - Scoring needs to be cheap (no full-attention recompute). They use a rolling attention proxy; need to validate cost on our runtime kernels.
  - How does this interact with prefix caching and partial KV reuse across threads? Risk: extra cache churn could hurt batching efficiency.
- Quick experiment: implement simple per-span score = alpha*recency + beta*max-attn-proxy; simulate eviction vs LRU on logs from 2029-09 production traces. Metrics: hit-rate by prefix length, tail latency 95/99, extra evictions per request.

2) "Quantization drift and fine-grained recalibration" (conference talk + repo) — notes
- Content: quantizing activations and attention matmul to 3–4 bits introduces subtle distributional shifts across layers; they propose small per-layer affine recalibration layers (2k parameters) learned on a calibration set to restore logits.
- Outcome: restores perplexity and downstream accuracy with almost no extra runtime cost.
- My take: fits neatly into Redwood Optimize as a safety fallback when enabling aggressive quant. A small learned adaptor could be shipped as a "quant-stability patch" that is applied at load time.
- Risks: calibration data domain mismatch can overfit; we should test across customer prompt families.
- Quick experiment: add per-layer 1D scale+bias to our quant loader for the 13B llama-derivative we test daily. Calibrate on dev prompts vs generic english vs domain-specific (finance) to measure sensitivity.

3) "Latency-aware continuous batching" (systems paper) — notes
- Idea: dynamically form batches using an online estimator of remaining per-request work (sequence length left + model variant cost) to keep latency SLOs while improving token throughput. Evict or forward requests to faster variant when SLO can't be met.
- Interesting detail: they used a small ML predictor for per-request runtime (10 features) and integrated with the scheduler for admission control.
- Where this maps to Redwood: we already have routing policies and fallback model variants. A lightweight per-request predictor could power smarter admission control in Dedicated pools.
- Quick to-dos:
  - Prototype predictor: features = [current_sequence_len, tokens_requested, model_variant_id, is_streaming_flag, cache_hit_estimate]. Train on annotated traces (we have 2 months). Evaluate accuracy and runtime overhead.
  - Simulate scheduler decisions offline before changing SRE heuristics.

4) "Mini-evals: cheap, frequent quality probes" (blog + open-source harness) — notes
- Summary: run a small battery of targeted evals per model rollout that measure specific failure surfaces (hallucination, calibration, instruction-following) using compact task suites (50–100 examples).
- Benefit: catches regressions faster than large eval suites; cheap enough to run on every canary.
- My idea: couple this with Redwood Console "rollout" UI so quality regressions incrementally block canary progression.
- Action: prototype a 4-metric mini-eval for our internal checkout: complexity, edit-distance, hallucination score (LM-based), and response latency. Hook to rollout pipeline.

Synthesis across reads:
- Common pattern: cheap local fixes (small learned recalibrators, eviction heuristics) often buy most of the value for production. The heavy lifts are in validation across varied prompt distributions.
- Operational risk: small changes can harm batching and KV cache hit patterns; must test at trace-replay scale.

Micro-experiments backlog (prioritized)
- EXP-001: "Span-score eviction" simulation on 2029-09 traces. (Owner: me)
  - Steps: implement scoring script + offline simulator, compare to token-LRU, produce hit-rate curves.
  - Success metric: >=10% improvement in useful-span hit-rate without increasing 99p latency by >5%.
- EXP-002: "Per-layer quant-recalibrator" proof-of-concept. (Owner: Mira)
  - Steps: implement loader hook, small calibration dataset, compare perplexity and few-shot QA on dev sets.
  - Success metric: recover >90% of fp16 accuracy for 3-bit quant on test suite.
- EXP-003: "Tiny predictor for latency admission". (Owner: Github PR #312)
  - Steps: featurize traces, train light tree model (<100KB), measure inference time of predictor, run offline scheduler sim.
- EXP-004: "Mini-eval Canary" integration into rollout job. (Owner: Owen)

Notes to self / heuristics to remember:
- When evaluating cache policies, always measure end-to-end user-turn quality (not just raw hit-rate). Small increases in hit-rate can be neutral or negative if hit content is low-signal.
- For quant tricks: always include a small domain-specific calibration set. Generic english calibrators bias toward common tokens and hide edge-case shifts.
- Batching improvements should be validated with realistic concurrency and connection churn patterns; microbenchmarks are misleading.

Resources and quick links (for my next 2 sessions)
- repos: github:redwood-inference/kv-cache-experiments (seed scripts + trace format)
- confluence: INF-PLAYBOOK-8743 (internal notes on cache simulator)
- slack thread: #kv-cache-playgrounds/thread-8421 (rtc logs and colleague questions)

Outstanding questions / open puzzles:
- Can we design a metric for "useful-span hit" that is automatable? Manual labels are expensive. Potential approach: LM-based relevance scorer anchored to next-turn tokens.
- How brittle are per-layer calibrators across model distillations (e.g., between 13B and 13B-quant-distilled)?
- If eviction increases prefix variability, can we compensate by adaptive batching windows? Or will that oscillate?

Next steps (this week)
- Monday: write simulator harness for span-scoring (2h) + schedule dataset pull.
- Tuesday: small PoC of per-layer calibrator in loader (Mira pair).
- Thursday: featurize 1 week of traces and run baseline predictor training (EXP-003).
- Friday: sync with Owen to sketch canary mini-eval integration.

Random scratch ideas (unpolished):
- "soft-evict" tag: mark low-score spans as deprioritized instead of removing immediately; allow a grace window to capture late-but-important tokens.
- lightweight "calibrator bank": for each customer with non-trivial usage, keep a 500-example calibration pack that can be applied to aggressive quant variants.

End of doc.

(Quick note: this is intentionally terse and pragmatic — meant as my working artifact more than a polished share. If something looks useful, I'll move it to confluence or a PR.)
